Leave-clade-out cross-validation

Source: R/loo_group.R
loo_group.Rd

Leave-one-out mostly asks how well a species is predicted from its closest relatives. Leaving out whole clades (or any other groups, such as orders or families) asks a harder question that bears more directly on the evolutionary process: how well does the model predict a group of species from the rest of the tree?

Usage

loo_group(fit, groups, ndraws = 400, ...)

Arguments

fit

A Bayesian phylogp_fit.

groups

A vector giving the group of each species, named by species (tip label), or an unnamed vector in the order of the data rows used in the fit (rownames(fit$data)).

ndraws

Number of posterior draws of each refit used.

...

Further arguments to $sample().

Value

An object of class c("kfold", "loo") usable with loo::loo_compare(): estimates of the expected log predictive density summed over groups (elpd_kfold), and a pointwise matrix with one row per group. The attribute groups gives group names and sizes, and species_elpd the marginal predictive density of each left-out species.

Details

For each group the model is refitted without the group's data (its species are given a very large measurement error, so the tree and any latent values on it stay the same), and the joint predictive density of the group, log mean_s p(y_group | y_rest, theta_s), is computed. For branch-wise kernels this is the difference of two pruning likelihoods, so it costs O(N) per draw; dense kernels use dense conditioning.

References

Vehtari A., Gelman A., Gabry J. 2017. Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC. Statistics and Computing. 27:1413–1432.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
lco <- loo_group(fit, groups = setNames(d$order, rownames(d)))
loo::loo_compare(lco_model_a, lco_model_b)
} # }
